summary: American Protestants fought over biblical authority, miracles, and adapting theology to modern scholarship. The conflict divided denominations and helped distinguish later evangelical and mainline networks.
why: Disagreements over reading Scripture divided modern Protestants even when they shared beliefs about baptism and Communion.
facts: Harry Emerson Fosdick preached Shall the Fundamentalists Win? in 1922.
J. Gresham Machen argued that liberal Christianity changed the faith itself.
Machen helped establish Westminster Seminary in 1929.
The Orthodox Presbyterian Church formed in 1936.
disputed: Conservatives defended doctrinal continuity. Modernists sought credible Christian teaching alongside historical criticism and science. Neither camp represented all Protestants.

name: World Council of Churches
summary: Churches founded the World Council of Churches in Amsterdam as a fellowship for unity, witness, and service. Orthodox and Protestant churches cooperate without merging their denominations.
why: Ecumenical cooperation can include shared study of baptism and Eucharist while churches retain different sacramental rules.
facts: The first assembly brought together 147 member churches.
The WCC is a fellowship. Member churches retain their own authority.
The Catholic Church cooperates but is not a member.
Churches widely discussed its 1982 text Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry.

name: Independent evangelical churches
summary: Independent evangelical churches expanded through Bible teaching, conversion preaching, church planting, and contemporary worship. Some grew into megachurches, while others remained small congregations.
why: A church's lack of a denominational name does not imply a single theology of baptism or Communion.
facts: 1950 marks postwar growth, not the first independent church.
Megachurches commonly have at least 2,000 weekly worshippers and can also belong to denominations.
Pew found nondenominational Protestants were 7% of US adults in 2023-24. Confidence high for this survey.
Worldwide evangelical-independent totals lack one definition. Confidence low.
sacraments: Usually two ordinances, believers' baptism and symbolic Communion. Frequency varies. Some churches retain infant baptism or Christ's spiritual presence. Charismatic churches emphasize spiritual gifts.
today: Millions worldwide. Strongest in Americas, Africa, and Asia.
disputed: Parents represent common influences. Independent, evangelical, charismatic, and megachurch labels overlap, but each describes something different.

name: US mainline mergers
summary: American Protestant denominations reunited older branches or joined related traditions. These mergers created the UCC, United Methodist Church, PCUSA, and ELCA. Each retained its own sacramental tradition.
why: The family tree includes branches joining together as well as splitting apart.
facts: 1957 UCC joined Congregational Christian Churches with the Evangelical and Reformed Church.
1968 United Methodist Church joined Methodists with the Evangelical United Brethren.
1983 PCUSA reunited the Presbyterian Church in the US with the United Presbyterian Church in the USA.
1988 ELCA united the ALC, LCA, and Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches.

name: Charismatic renewal
summary: Christians brought Pentecostal-style prayer, healing, and spiritual gifts into existing denominations. Protestant renewal gained attention in 1960. Catholic renewal spread from Duquesne University in 1967.
why: Spiritual gifts can coexist with Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, or other established sacramental teaching.
facts: Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett publicized his experience of tongues in 1960.
The Duquesne Weekend helped begin Catholic charismatic renewal in February 1967.
Many participants stayed within their existing churches.
Charismatics share the 2026 combined 676M Pentecostal-charismatic estimate. Separate total uncertain. Confidence medium.
sacraments: Participants retain their churches' sacrament counts, baptism practices, and Eucharistic beliefs. Spirit baptism means spiritual renewal. Catholics do not count it as an additional sacrament.
today: Hundreds of millions across denominations worldwide. Counts overlap Pentecostals.
disputed: Participants belong to different denominations. The Pentecostal parent represents influence on their worship.

name: Vatican II
summary: The Catholic council renewed worship, encouraged lay participation, and committed Catholics to dialogue with other Christians. It permitted wider use of local languages. Later reforms changed the Mass.
why: The council allowed wider use of local languages in Catholic worship and encouraged dialogue with other Christians.
facts: John XXIII opened the council. Paul VI completed it.
Sacrosanctum Concilium authorized expanded vernacular use while preserving Latin in principle.
Unitatis Redintegratio addressed Christian unity in 1964.
The reformed Roman Missal followed in 1969 and 1970.
sacraments: The council retained seven sacraments, baptismal grace, transubstantiation, and Eucharistic sacrifice. It promoted active participation, Scripture readings, and approved liturgy in local languages.
disputed: Catholics dispute some later interpretations and reforms. The council itself did not abolish Latin or redefine the Eucharist as merely symbolic.

name: 1054 excommunications lifted
summary: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras removed the 1054 excommunications from church memory. Their joint declaration encouraged Catholic-Orthodox reconciliation. The churches remained divided.
why: Reconciliation gestures and theological dialogue can advance without making Catholic and Orthodox Communion interchangeable.
facts: The declaration appeared on December 7, 1965.
The original censures targeted particular people, not every member of both churches.
Both sides regretted the words and actions that deepened estrangement.
Lifting the censures did not end the schism or restore shared Eucharistic communion.

name: Joint declaration on justification
summary: The Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church agreed on basic truths about justification by God's grace through faith. They judged earlier condemnations inapplicable to the agreed teaching.
why: A central Reformation disagreement narrowed, while differences about church authority, ministry, and sacraments remained.
facts: Representatives signed the declaration in Augsburg on October 31, 1999.
The agreement describes a consensus in basic truths, not identical theology on every point.
It did not create full church communion or general permission for shared Eucharist.
Some Lutheran churches outside the federation reject the agreement.
disputed: Supporters see doctrinal agreement. Critics argue that important differences remain or that the document weakens Lutheran teaching.

name: GAFCON Anglican realignment
summary: Conservative Anglican leaders organized GAFCON amid conflicts over sexuality and biblical authority. They supported ACNA and later claimed to reorganize global Anglican communion beyond Canterbury's institutions.
why: Anglican identity now depends on disputed relationships between provinces, shared doctrine, and Communion institutions.
facts: GAFCON met in Jerusalem and issued its declaration in 2008.
It supported ACNA's formation in 2009.
GAFCON announced its Global Anglican Communion initiative in October 2025.
The March 2026 Abuja Affirmation rejected Canterbury's governing instruments. Confidence high for GAFCON's stated position.
disputed: GAFCON claims to restore historic Anglican faith. Other Anglicans dispute its authority and its claim to speak for the Communion.

name: ACNA
summary: The Anglican Church in North America united conservative Anglican groups, including congregations leaving Episcopal and Canadian Anglican churches. Several overseas Anglican provinces recognized the new body.
why: An Anglican church can retain its liturgy and sacraments while changing which bishops and provinces it recognizes.
facts: ACNA formed in 2009.
Conflicts included sexuality, biblical authority, and episcopal oversight.
Recognition by overseas provinces does not equal membership in Canterbury's Anglican Communion institutions.
Its current official welcome page reports over 130,000 members. Confidence medium for this rounded claim.
sacraments: Two principal sacraments, baptism and Eucharist, plus five sacramental rites. Churches baptize infants. Eucharistic teaching ranges from Reformed spiritual presence to Anglo-Catholic real presence.
today: Over 130,000 reported members. United States, Canada, and Latin America.
disputed: ACNA calls itself an Anglican province. Its status within the wider Communion remains contested.

name: Moscow-Constantinople communion break
summary: Moscow ended Eucharistic communion with Constantinople over its decisions concerning Ukraine. The Orthodox Church of Ukraine's later independence deepened disputes over church boundaries and recognition.
why: Orthodox churches can share sacramental beliefs while refusing Eucharistic communion because they dispute who has authority over a territory.
facts: Moscow's Holy Synod announced the break on October 15, 2018.
Constantinople had moved toward Ukrainian autocephaly and restored previously excluded Ukrainian hierarchs.
The OCU formed in December 2018 and received its tomos in January 2019.
This was a jurisdictional rupture inside Orthodoxy, not a new creed or sacramental system.
sacraments: Both retain Orthodox baptism and Eucharistic real presence. Moscow forbids its clergy and faithful from receiving Communion in Constantinople's churches.
disputed: Moscow claims authority in Ukraine. Constantinople disputes that claim and asserts authority to grant church independence. Orthodox churches differ over recognition.

name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
summary: A Kyiv council united Ukrainian Orthodox groups in December 2018. Patriarch Bartholomew granted the new church independence in January 2019. Moscow rejects that decision.
why: A self-governing Orthodox church retains Orthodox beliefs and sacraments. Disputes over its independence affect which churches share Communion with it.
facts: The unification council elected Metropolitan Epiphanius in December 2018.
Bartholomew signed the tomos on January 5 and presented it on January 6, 2019.
It is distinct from the Ukrainian Orthodox Church historically linked to Moscow.
Razumkov's 2024 survey found 35% identifying with OCU. Confidence medium. This is identification, not membership.
sacraments: Orthodox mysteries, commonly counted as seven. Infants receive baptism, chrismation, and Communion. The church teaches Eucharistic real presence. Church independence concerns governance.
today: Millions identify with OCU in Ukraine. Exact membership uncertain.
disputed: Constantinople recognizes its autocephaly. Moscow rejects it. Orthodox recognition is partial, so communion depends on the particular church.

name: United Methodist split
summary: Disputes over sexuality, biblical authority, and enforcing church rules led thousands of congregations to leave the United Methodist Church. Many joined the Global Methodist Church.
why: Both churches kept Methodist sacraments. The split chiefly changed church affiliation and rules about marriage and ordination.
facts: The 2019 General Conference strengthened restrictions and authorized a temporary US disaffiliation process.
The Global Methodist Church launched on May 1, 2022.
About 7,600 US congregations left in 2019-2023. Not all joined the GMC.
UMC removed bans on gay clergy and same-sex weddings in 2024. Confidence high.
disputed: Conservatives emphasize biblical authority and continuity. Supporters of inclusion emphasize equal participation. Departing congregations chose several destinations.

name: Global Methodist Church
summary: Conservative Methodists formed a new denomination as United Methodist divisions widened. The Global Methodist Church retains Wesleyan theology and teaches marriage between a man and a woman.
why: Its doctrinal separation concerns authority and sexual ethics more than baptism or Eucharistic presence.
facts: The denomination launched on May 1, 2022.
Its convening General Conference met in Costa Rica in September 2024.
Its doctrine retains infant baptism and two sacraments as means of grace.
The church reported 7,250 congregations in September 2026. No global adherent total accompanies that report.
Its next General Conference met in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2026.
sacraments: Two sacraments, infant or adult baptism and Holy Communion. Communion conveys grace and Christ's body and blood spiritually through faith. Bread and wine remain unchanged.
today: 7,250 congregations reported in September 2026. Global adherent total unverified.

name: Nicaea 1700th anniversary
summary: Pope Leo XIV, Patriarch Bartholomew, and other Christian leaders prayed at Iznik on November 28, 2025. They commemorated 1,700 years since the first Council of Nicaea.
why: The Nicene faith remains shared across major Christian traditions even where church government and Eucharistic communion remain divided.
facts: Iznik in Türkiye is ancient Nicaea, the council's meeting place in 325.
Leaders gathered near the archaeological remains of Saint Neophytos Basilica.
They commemorated shared faith and prayed for Christian unity.
Vatican and independent reports confirm the completed November 2025 gathering. Confidence high.

name: Christianity today
summary: Catholic, Protestant, independent, Eastern Orthodox, and Oriental Orthodox churches remain distinct in October 2026. Counts differ by membership definitions, reference year, and how researchers count overlapping movements.
why: These figures give an approximate sense of size. Membership totals do not measure agreement about Christian beliefs.
facts: The Vatican reports 1.422B baptized Catholics for 2024.
WCD estimates 1.06B Protestants and independents in 2026, including Pentecostal churches.
WCD estimates 293M Orthodox Christians in 2026, combining Eastern and Oriental churches.
Pentecostal and charismatic counts overlap denominations. These totals use different sources and cannot form a consistent global sum.
disputed: The Vatican counts baptized Catholics. WCD uses different definitions. Subtracting totals from different sources cannot reliably count Eastern Orthodox.
